newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian outback election faces race issue.
newsitem.headline: Australian outback election faces race issue.

text.p: Campaigning in Australia's vast outback Northern Territory for an August 30 poll began on Wednesday with politicians and Aborigines warning the divisive issue of race will dominate the election.

The poll is the first since Australia became engulfed in a bitter race debate last September, sparked by independent politician Pauline Hanson and fuelled by the emergence of Aboriginal native title on farm lands.

It will be an electoral test for native title, which conservative Prime Minister John Howard is attempting to extinquish in the face of bitter opposition from Aborigines, human rights officials and churches
The Northern Territory, which is more than five times the size of Britain and home to the highest per capita number of Aborigines in Australia, is familiar with race politics.
"The race card is always played here by the conservatives and quite successfully in the urban areas," Labor opposition leader Maggie Hickey told Reuters from Darwin.
Labor has never won an election in the territory, which has a scattered population of 190,000, a quarter of whom are Aborigines.
Aboriginal leaders told talk-back radio in Darwin that they too feared "black bashing" would dominate the short campaign, just as in previous elections.
"We've got the redneck element in the territory. We have the odd chapter of the Klu Klux Klan," Tracker Tilmouth, Central Lands Council director, said in a radio interview.
"Unfortunately people listen to them and they really represent a minority," Tilmouth said.

Northern Territory Chief Minister Shane Stone announced the poll on Tuesday, declaring native title a major issue and warning that unless it was extinquished, 7,000 jobs in the territory would be lost.

Stone said 80 percent of the territory's 1.34 million sq km (519,770 sq miles) was vulnerable to native title. Aborigines already control 50 percent of the territory under existing land rights laws which give them inalienable freehold title.
Newspapers on Wednesday declared: "Stone plays native title card", but Stone denied he was making race an issue.
"I don't accept there is a race card," Stone told reporters.
"Important issues like native title and land rights are entitled to be aired in this community because in the Northern Territory it is a matter of vital concern."
Historically, the ruling Country Liberal Party (CLP) has campaigned heavily on racial issues in the territory, which it has governed uninterrupted for 19 years.

The CLP traditionally claims that Aboriginal land rights represent a threat to the territory's comfortable lifestyle -- a strategy aimed at the majority of voters who live in the territory's two cities, Darwin and Alice Springs.
There are an estimated 300,000 Aborigines among Australia's 18 million people. Aborigines have a life expectancy 15 to 20 years less than other Australians.

The territory is predominately desert, but has rich mineral deposits on Aboriginal land. Aborigines in the territory gained land rights in 1976 and remain the only indigenous people in Australia to hold inalienable land rights.
In 1993, Australia's then Labor government passed native title laws after a court ruled that Aborigines had ownership of land prior to European settlement in 1788.

Native title was thought to only cover unused government land, but in 1996 the High Court of Australia ruled native title could co-exist with farmers' rights, sparking warnings from farmers that their livelihoods were at risk.
